title: Comparison of traditional and ecological dynamical training approaches in Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu: effects on Force Development, reactivity, and distress perception
authors: Giuseppe Giardullo, Rosario Ceruso, Giuseppe Di Lascio, Manuele Taleb, Giovanni Esposito, and Francesca D’Elia

population.ageGroup: amateur and semi-professional BJJ athletes ages 18–40

intervention.description: Ecological-dynamical training compared with a traditional approach

tested: Force development, response time to a light stimulus, and self-reported distress after the training period.
found: The ecological-dynamical group improved more on the measured force, light-response, and distress outcomes in this sample.
notTested: Live grappling skill, delayed retention, transfer to new situations, children, beginners, or Sensei Sandy BJJ classes. The distress questionnaire was ad hoc and had no external psychometric validation.
supports: A bounded report of the measured outcomes in these adult athletes
doesNotSupport: Claims of better live grappling skill or long-term learning
cardSummary: After eight weeks, the game group did better on some force and light-response tests. Its distress report also changed.
cardLimit: The study did not test live BJJ skill or how long skills last. It did not study kids, new learners, or our school.

title: The effect of game-based approaches on decision-making, knowledge, and motor skill: A systematic review and a multilevel meta-analysis
authors: Manninen M, Magrum E, Campbell S, and Belton S

population.ageGroup: physical education learners across included studies

intervention.description: Games-based teaching approaches in physical education and sport

tested: Outcomes included game decision-making, motor-skill tests, knowledge, and motor skill during games.
found: The review reported better game-decision and motor-skill test results, but not better knowledge or motor skill measured during games.
notTested: Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu classes or Sensei Sandy BJJ teaching. Findings do not establish one best approach for every learner or sport.
supports: A qualified summary of selected physical-education outcomes across the included studies
doesNotSupport: One teaching approach winning in every setting
cardLabel: Review of studies · other sports · 28 studies · 2024/2025
cardSummary: A review of 28 studies with 1,600 people found gains on some game-choice and skill tests.
cardLimit: Not every test showed a gain. These studies were not about BJJ.

title: How do students learn to move? A systematic review of collaborative and game-based pedagogies in physical education
authors: Saha S, İlbak İ, Abdi E, Deutsch J, Katanić B, Choudhary S, Choudhary PK, Souza LN, Silva Júnior RR, and Tornóczky GJ

population.ageGroup: physical education and PETE participants in included studies

intervention.description: Game-based and comparison teaching approaches in physical education

tested: Motor-skill and game-performance results across quasi-experimental PE/PETE studies.
found: Seven studies reported significant motor or game-performance improvement, five reported mixed results, and five found no motor-skill advantage. Methods and outcomes varied; there was no pooled effect estimate.
notTested: BJJ classes or Sensei Sandy BJJ teaching. The varied evidence does not identify one approach that wins in all settings.
supports: A cautious summary of varied PE/PETE study results
cardLabel: Review of studies · other sports · 17 studies · 2026
cardSummary: Seven studies found clear gains, five had mixed results, and five found no better result.
cardLimit: The studies used many games and tests. They did not study BJJ.

title: Designing challenge for discovery in skill learning: toward self-regulated and representative adaptation

intervention.description: Conceptual perspective on matching learning challenge to the learner, task, and setting

tested: No intervention was tested; this is a perspective article.
found: The authors argue that challenge should fit the learner, task, and context, and that learning can be considered through retention, transfer, adaptability, and self-regulation.
notTested: No BJJ teaching method or learner outcome. This perspective does not demonstrate that a specific SSBJJ class method works.
supports: Explaining an expert framework for thinking about task challenge
cardTitle: How hard should a game be?
cardSummary: The authors say a task should fit what a learner can do now.
cardLimit: This paper shares ideas. It did not test a BJJ class or show that one way is best.

title: Effects of a school-based Brazilian jiu-jitsu programme on mental health and classroom behaviour of children from Abu Dhabi: a randomised trial

intervention.description: Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu compared with regular physical education

tested: Teacher-rated behavioral outcomes in one Abu Dhabi school program.
found: Teacher-rated emotional symptoms (p=.007), hyperactivity and inattention (p<.001), total difficulties (p=.002), and externalizing behavior (p=.001, η²=.07) differed on selected measures.
notTested: ADHD treatment, every child, or Sensei Sandy BJJ classes. Results do not promise an individual outcome.
supports: Selected teacher-rated behavioral outcomes in this study population
authors: Jean Carlo Benetti Bueno, Leonardo Vidal Andreato, Rodrigo Batalha Silva, and Alexandro Andrade
cardLabel: BJJ study · 2022 online / 2023 issue · 88 enrolled · 80 analyzed
cardSummary: In one school study, some teacher-rated behavior scores changed more after BJJ than PE.
cardLimit: This was one school study of boys. It used teacher reports. It did not test our school or show what each child will gain.
detailedResults: The reported values were p=.007 for emotional symptoms, p<.001 for hyperactivity/inattention, p=.002 for total difficulties, and p=.001 with η²=.07 for externalizing behavior.

title: Does Taekwondo Improve Children’s Self-Regulation? If so, How? A Randomized Field Experiment
authors: Terry Ng-Knight, Katie A. Gilligan-Lee, Jessica Massonnié, Hanna Gaspard, Debbie Gooch, Dawn Querstret, and Nicola Johnstone

intervention.description: Taekwondo compared with active physical education

tested: Attention and behavior outcomes in a Taekwondo trial.
found: Some teacher-rated conduct and child self-regulation measures changed; the executive-attention effect was about d=.28 and conduct-problem rate ratio was .79. Not every measured outcome improved.
notTested: BJJ classes or Sensei Sandy BJJ teaching. Taekwondo findings are not BJJ findings, and not every measured outcome improved.
supports: Cautious martial-arts context for selected attention outcomes
cardSummary: A study of 240 children ages 7 to 11 found changes in some focus and behavior scores.
cardLimit: This was Taekwondo, not BJJ. Not all tests improved. It cannot show that BJJ has the same result.
detailedResults: The source reports an executive-attention effect of about d=.28 and a conduct-problem incidence-rate ratio of .79.

title: Effects of open-skill exercise on executive functions in children and adolescents: a systematic review and meta-analysis
authors: Shunding Hu, Peng Shi, Ziyun Zhang, Xiaosu Feng, Kai Zhang, and Teng Jin
tested: Selected executive-function outcomes across open-skill exercise studies.
found: The review reported selected executive-function results in the broader open-skill exercise category.
notTested: Sensei Sandy BJJ classes, BJJ superiority to soccer, or an individual outcome guarantee.
supports: Selected executive-function outcomes in the broader open-skill category
cardLabel: Review of studies · other sports · online 2025 / 2024 volume · 17 studies
cardSummary: A review of 17 studies with 1,298 young people found changes in some thinking scores.
cardLimit: The review covered many sports. It did not test our school or show that BJJ is better than other sports.
detailedResults: The review included 17 studies (11 randomized) and 1,298 children and adolescents ages 5–16. It reported selected pooled executive-function results with high heterogeneity.

title: Characterization of Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu training effects on the physical fitness of men and women
authors: Leandro Lourenço-Lima, Tácito P. Souza-Junior, Alexandre R. Okuyama, Steven R. McAnulty, Alan C. Utter, Thaísa S. Monteiro, Gustavo Barquilha, José R. Bortolon, Tatiana P. Geraldo, and Sandro M. Hirabara
tested: Body mass, body composition, aerobic and anaerobic power, strength, and flexibility before and after six weeks of training.
found: Some fitness measures changed; body mass and body composition did not.
notTested: BJJ superiority to Pilates, long-term results, or individual fitness outcomes.
supports: Describing regular BJJ practice as physical training
cardSummary: In a small study, some fitness scores changed after six weeks of BJJ classes.
cardLimit: Only 16 adults took part. The study cannot show that BJJ beats other exercise or change each person’s fitness.
detailedResults: The report found changes in VO₂max, time to exhaustion, lower-body strength, and several anaerobic measures. Body mass and body composition did not change.

title: Modern unexplored martial arts – what can mixed martial arts and Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu do for youth development?

intervention.description: Participants self-selected Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu or mixed martial arts; sport was not randomly assigned

tested: Self-control, prosocial behavior, and aggression before and after participation.
found: Both groups reported increased self-control and prosocial behavior. Aggression-score directions differed, and the MMA group began with higher aggression scores.
notTested: Whether sport caused the changes, every youth participant, or Sensei Sandy BJJ classes.
supports: Reporting group-level behavioral findings with observational limits
doesNotSupport: Causal claims that either sport caused behavior changes
Generalizing results to all youth or Sensei Sandy BJJ
cardLabel: BJJ and MMA study · 2020 issue · 113 people
cardSummary: Both groups said some self-control and social scores went up. Aggression scores changed in different ways.
cardLimit: People chose their sport. The study cannot show that either sport caused the changes.

displayLabel: Ecological-dynamic and active-reflection rugby study (additional reading)

population.ageGroup: boys ages 12–14 playing U14 rugby; 20 per group

intervention.description: Ecological-dynamic training with active reflection compared with traditional rugby training

tested: Coordination, fitness, attention, concentration, executive function, and workload.
found: The ecological-dynamic group improved more on some motor, cognitive, and perception tests. The groups did not differ on physiological measures.
notTested: Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu, Sensei Sandy BJJ classes, or the effect of live tasks without active reflection. The study tested a combined approach in a small group of boys.
supports: A bounded report of this two-group study with young rugby players
doesNotSupport: Separating the effect of games from active reflection
title: Systemic relationships between ecological-dynamic approach and active reflection: psycho-neuro-motor, cognitive, and physiological interactions in rugby pedagogy
authors: Marta Rigon, Raffaele Scurati, Giampiero Merati, Damiano Formenti, Athos Trecroci, Pietro Luigi Invernizzi, and Gabriele Signorini
moreReadingSummary: 40 boys ages 12–14; other sport, not BJJ.

intervention.description: Review of ecological-dynamic motor-learning theory and applied work
